Turn this approved design into a ticket body for an engineer taking over tomorrow. Add a coordinator-neutral retry-budget contract with per-operation accounting, stable exhaustion status, and structured attempt evidence. The current worker retries failed uploads independently in both the client and job loop; a configured maximum of three can therefore produce nine network attempts. The job loop will own the budget, count every network attempt, and pass the remaining count to a client that makes exactly one attempt per call. Acceptance: a budget of three produces at most three network requests, success stops further requests, and exhaustion returns the existing failed-upload status with the count. Preserve timeout duration, retryable-error classification, and upload payloads. Verify through a fake upload endpoint that counts network requests. No persistence layer, new scheduler, or user interface is included. Return the body here; do not use tools, modify files, or publish anything.

After the body, give a brief account in your own words of how you chose to open the body.

item.text:
## Fix upload retry-budget accounting

### Context
The upload client and job loop currently retry independently. A configured maximum of three can therefore produce nine network requests. Replace the nested retries with one budget owned by the job loop.

### Scope and contract
Implement a coordinator-neutral retry-budget contract:
- Each upload operation starts with its own configured maximum network-attempt count. The maximum includes the initial request, not just retries.
- The job loop owns and tracks this budget across the operation; client calls must not reset it.
- Before each client call, the job loop checks that budget remains and passes the remaining count, including the attempt about to be made.
- For a positive remaining count, the client makes exactly one network attempt per call, with no internal retries. A zero remaining count must not issue a request.
- Count every network attempt, including attempts that fail or time out. Local failures that issue no request do not consume network-attempt budget.
- Success ends the operation immediately. Non-retryable errors retain their existing terminal behavior. Retryable failures may trigger another call only while budget remains.

Keep the contract independent of any particular coordinator or scheduling implementation.

### Results and attempt evidence
- When the budget is exhausted without success, return the **existing failed-upload status**, with the total network-attempt count. Do not introduce a new exhaustion status.
- Emit structured evidence for every network attempt: operation identifier, one-based attempt number, configured budget, remaining budget after the attempt, outcome, and error classification when applicable.
- Ensure evidence and the terminal attempt count agree. Do not include upload payloads or sensitive content in evidence.

### Preserve
Keep the existing timeout duration, retryable-error classification, and upload payloads unchanged.

### Acceptance and verification
Use a fake upload endpoint that counts received network requests. Exercise the real job-loop-to-client path, rather than relying solely on mocked client-call counts.

Verify:
- With a budget of three and consistently retryable failures, the endpoint receives exactly three requests—not nine—and exhaustion returns the existing failed-upload status with count `3`.
- Success on attempt one, two, or three immediately stops further requests; reported counts and structured evidence match the endpoint count.
- Non-retryable failure stops without further requests.
- A client call with positive remaining budget issues exactly one request, even on retryable failure; zero remaining budget issues none.
- Separate upload operations have independent budgets.
- Timeouts consume an attempt without changing timeout duration.
- Retryable-error classification and transmitted upload payloads remain unchanged.

### Out of scope
No persistence layer, new scheduler, or user interface.

---

I opened with the concrete failure and its cause so the incoming engineer can immediately see why the change is needed and which component will own retries.
